interactive_questions.explanation: CRISPR-Cas9 uses guide RNA to direct the Cas9 enzyme to a specific DNA location, where it cuts both strands, allowing precise gene editing through cellular repair mechanisms.

theory.title: CRISPR-Cas9 Mechanism
theory.content:
CRISPR-Cas9 is a powerful tool for editing genomes. It allows researchers to easily alter DNA sequences and modify gene function.

The system consists of two key molecules that introduce a change into the DNA:

  • Cas9: An enzyme that acts as a pair of 'molecular scissors' that can cut the two strands of DNA at a specific location.
  • Guide RNA (gRNA): A small piece of pre-designed RNA sequence located within a longer RNA scaffold. The scaffold part binds to DNA and the pre-designed sequence 'guides' Cas9 to the right part of the genome.

interactive_questions.title: What is CRISPR?
options: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats
Cellular RNA Integration Sequence Protocol Repair
Chromosomal Recombination In Specific Protein Regions
Controlled Replication of Inserted Sequences for Proteins
interactive_questions.answer: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats
interactive_questions.explanation: CRISPR stands for Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats - naturally occurring sequences in bacterial DNA that inspired the gene-editing technology.

theory.title: The Origins of CRISPR
theory.content:
CRISPR stands for Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats.

These are unique sequences found in the DNA of bacteria and archaea. They are the hallmark of a bacterial defense system that forms the basis for CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing technology.

interactive_questions.title: Cas9 Enzyme
interactive_questions.prompt: What is the function of Cas9 in the CRISPR system?
options: It acts as molecular scissors to cut DNA
interactive_questions.answer: It acts as molecular scissors to cut DNA
interactive_questions.explanation: Cas9 is an endonuclease enzyme that acts as 'molecular scissors,' cutting both strands of DNA at the location specified by the guide RNA.

theory.title: Cas9: The Molecular Scissors
theory.content:
Cas9 (CRISPR-associated protein 9) is an enzyme that acts like a pair of molecular scissors, capable of cutting strands of DNA.

Although Cas9 is the enzyme that cuts the DNA, it needs a guide to tell it where to cut. This guide is the gRNA.

interactive_questions.title: Polymerase Chain Reaction
interactive_questions.prompt: Which technique is used to make multiple copies of a DNA segment?
interactive_questions.explanation: PCR amplifies DNA by using thermal cycling and DNA polymerase to create millions of copies of a specific DNA segment in just a few hours.

theory.title: Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)
theory.content:
PCR is a technique used to 'amplify' - copy - small segments of DNA.

Using PCR, copies of DNA sequences are exponentially amplified to generate thousands to millions of more copies of that particular DNA segment. This is crucial for many genetic engineering procedures.

interactive_questions.title: Recombinant DNA
options: Joining DNA from different sources using restriction enzymes and ligase
interactive_questions.answer: Joining DNA from different sources using restriction enzymes and ligase
interactive_questions.explanation: Recombinant DNA technology uses restriction enzymes to cut DNA at specific sites and DNA ligase to join fragments from different sources, creating new genetic combinations.

theory.title: Recombinant DNA Technology
theory.content:
Recombinant DNA (rDNA) molecules are DNA molecules formed by laboratory methods of genetic recombination (such as molecular cloning) to bring together genetic material from multiple sources, creating sequences that would not otherwise be found in the genome.

Key tools include restriction enzymes (to cut DNA) and DNA ligase (to join DNA fragments).

interactive_questions.title: PCR Amplification Math
interactive_questions.prompt: Explore the exponential growth of DNA during Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR).
interactive_questions.explanation: PCR doubles the DNA copies each cycle, leading to exponential growth.

theory.title: PCR Exponential Growth
theory.content:
Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) is a method used to rapidly make millions to billions of copies of a specific DNA sample.

Because each cycle doubles the amount of DNA, the growth is exponential. This allows scientists to take a very small sample of DNA and amplify it to a large enough amount to study in detail.
